voice.reference_text: 大家好，欢迎来到 AI 高频词。每一期，我们只讲清楚一个词：它解决什么问题，怎么理解它，以及它在现实里意味着什么。

items.text: Last time, we said a model is a machine with knobs, and learning means turning those knobs to the right spot.
But what does "right" even mean? How does the machine know this turn beat the last one?
The trick is to give its mistakes a score.
That score is called the loss, and the rule for working it out is the loss function. That's today's topic.
Every time the model guesses, it lands a bit too high or too low. That gap is the error.
Roll all those errors up into one number, and that's the loss: a score for how wrong it is.
It's the opposite of a test score: lower is better, and zero means not wrong at all.
Kind of like golf, where fewer strokes is better.
Now the machine can check itself. If a turn lowers the score, keep it. If not, turn it back.
So training is just turning the knobs again and again to push that score down.
Remember those twelve made-up taxi rides? Distance along the bottom, fare up the side.
The model's still that straight line, with two knobs: starting fare and price per kilometer.
First try: a five-dollar starting fare and two dollars a kilometer. The whole line sits too low.
Take the five-kilometer ride: it cost twenty-three dollars, the model guessed fifteen, so it's off by eight. That's the error.
Now square it: eight times eight is sixty-four. That's the red square.
Do that for all twelve rides, take the average, and this setting scores seventy-eight.
Second try: four dollars to start and three fifty a kilometer. Too steep, so short rides come out low and long ones high.
If we skip the squaring and just average the errors, the lows and the highs cancel out.
The average is only minus thirty-three cents, so it looks like it's barely wrong at all.
So we square. Everything turns positive, and nothing cancels.
And big misses cost way more: off by two costs four, but off by eight costs sixty-four.
Square, then average, and this setting scores thirteen point four.
This is called mean squared error, and it's one of the most common loss functions.
Third try: ten dollars to start, two fifty a kilometer. The squares are tiny, and it scores two point one nine.
The third has the lowest score, so it's the best of the three.
But that's only three tries. Score every setting of both knobs, and you get a landscape of scores.
Starting fare along the bottom, price per kilometer up the side, and the darker the color, the higher the score.
Our three tries: the first way up high, the second halfway down, the third nearly at the bottom of the valley.
The best is ten dollars twenty to start and two fifty-four a kilometer. It scores one point nine seven.
It's the best setting, and the whole job of training is finding that lowest point.
Here's something easy to miss: even the lowest point isn't zero.
Real fares bounce around with traffic and detours, so no straight line could nail every ride.
Training isn't chasing zero. It's getting as low as it can.
Here's the thing: the model has no idea what a taxi is. All it sees is the score.
The way you score it shapes how it learns. Because we squared the errors, it's terrified of big mistakes.
It would rather be a little off on every ride than way off on just one.
So when you pick a loss function, you're really telling the model what "good" means.
Big language models like ChatGPT get a score in training too, just not for taxi fares.
Their job is to guess the next word, like what comes after "Twinkle, twinkle, little."
The score checks how sure the model was about the real next word. The less sure, the bigger the penalty.
If it was ninety percent sure of the right word, the penalty's tiny. Only ten percent sure, and it's way bigger.
This kind of scoring is called cross-entropy. The name is all you need for now.
In twenty twenty-three, Meta tracked that score while training a model called Llama 2.
It read two trillion tokens of text. Tokens are roughly words or bits of words.
And even then, the score was still falling, nowhere near flat.
A big model has tens of billions of knobs, we have two, but the job's the same: find the lowest point.
So, a loss function is how you score the model's mistakes, and lower is better.
And training is just pushing that score down.
But with tons of knobs, that landscape's way too big to see all at once. So which way do you turn to go downhill?
That's where gradient descent comes in. It's up next time.
